title: Cost and Management Accounting (Inter P4)
description: ICAI Intermediate Paper 4 (new scheme) for May 2027 onward: cost sheets, material, employee and overhead costing, ABC, costing systems, job to process costing, standard and marginal costing, and budgets. Heavy on worked numericals in ICAI exam style.

chapters.title: Introduction to Cost and Management Accounting
chapters.summary: Cost objects, cost units and centres, classification of costs and the cost sheet that every later chapter builds on.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Cost, costing and cost management
lesson.body:
**Cost** is the amount of expenditure (actual or notional) incurred on, or attributable to, a given thing. **Costing** is the technique of ascertaining cost. **Cost accounting** records, classifies and allocates costs so that management can price, control and decide. **Management accounting** uses cost and financial data for planning, control and decision making.

The vocabulary you must use precisely in the exam:

- **Cost object**: anything for which a separate cost measurement is wanted: a product, a job, a customer, a department, a project.
- **Cost unit**: the unit of product or service in which cost is expressed: per tonne (steel), per kWh (power), per passenger-km (bus), per patient-day (hospital), per 1,000 bricks.
- **Cost centre**: the smallest segment of activity for which costs are collected: a machine, a department, a person. Production cost centres make the product; service cost centres (stores, maintenance, canteen) support them. A centre can be personal (a person) or impersonal (a location or machine).
- **Responsibility centres**: cost centre (manager answers for costs), revenue centre (for revenue), profit centre (for both), investment centre (for profit and capital employed, judged on ROI or residual income).

lesson.heading: Classification of costs
lesson.body:
Costs are classified on several bases at once. The same rent can be indirect (by traceability), fixed (by behaviour) and a factory overhead (by function).

| Basis | Classes | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature or element | Material, employee cost, expenses | Steel, wages, power |
| Traceability | Direct, indirect | Wood in a table (direct); factory rent (indirect) |
| Function | Production, administration, selling, distribution, R&D | Showroom rent is selling |
| Behaviour (variability) | Fixed, variable, semi-variable, step | Telephone bill with rental plus call charges is semi-variable |
| Controllability | Controllable, uncontrollable | Material usage is controllable by the shop manager |
| Normality | Normal, abnormal | Normal idle time vs strike |
| Decision making | Relevant, sunk, opportunity, differential, out-of-pocket, imputed | Rent forgone on own building is an opportunity cost |

**Semi-variable costs** are split with the **high-low method**: variable cost per unit = change in cost / change in activity; fixed cost = total cost at either level - variable portion.

Remember that fixed cost is fixed **in total** within the relevant range; fixed cost **per unit** falls as output rises. Variable cost is constant **per unit** and varies in total.

lesson.heading: The cost sheet format
lesson.body:
The cost sheet (statement of cost) builds cost up in layers. Learn the ICAI layout:

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Opening stock of raw material + purchases + carriage inward - closing stock | xxx |
| **Direct material consumed** | xxx |
| Direct employee (labour) cost | xxx |
| Direct expenses (hire of special machine, royalty on production) | xxx |
| **Prime cost** | xxx |
| Add: Factory (works) overheads | xxx |
| Add: Opening WIP - Less: Closing WIP | xxx |
| **Works (factory) cost** | xxx |
| Add: Quality control, R&D (process related), administration overheads relating to production, primary packing | xxx |
| Less: Credit for recoveries (sale of scrap) | (xxx) |
| **Cost of production** | xxx |
| Add: Opening finished goods - Less: Closing finished goods | xxx |
| **Cost of goods sold** | xxx |
| Add: General administration overheads, selling and distribution overheads (including secondary packing) | xxx |
| **Cost of sales** | xxx |
| Profit (balancing figure) | xxx |
| **Sales** | xxx |

Primary packing (the container the product cannot be sold without) is part of cost of production. Secondary packing (outer cartons for transport, attractive packing for display) is selling or distribution.

lesson.heading: Worked example and tender pricing
lesson.body:
Last year a firm had direct material ₹6,00,000, direct wages ₹4,00,000, works overheads ₹2,40,000 and office overheads ₹1,24,000. For a tender needing material ₹50,000 and wages ₹30,000, first derive the recovery rates from past data:

- Works overheads as % of direct wages = 2,40,000 / 4,00,000 = 60%
- Office overheads as % of works cost = 1,24,000 / 12,40,000 = 10%

| Tender cost | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Material | 50,000 |
| Wages | 30,000 |
| Works overheads (60% of wages) | 18,000 |
| **Works cost** | **98,000** |
| Office overheads (10% of works cost) | 9,800 |
| **Total cost** | **1,07,800** |
| Profit (20% on price = 25% on cost) | 26,950 |
| **Quoted price** | **1,34,750** |

Common mistakes:

- Adding closing WIP instead of deducting it, or adjusting WIP after works cost.
- Valuing closing finished goods at cost of sales instead of cost of production.
- Treating "20% profit on selling price" as 20% on cost. 20% on price = 25% on cost.
- Putting secondary packing or general administration inside cost of production.

keyPoints: Prime cost = direct material + direct employee cost + direct expenses.
Works cost = prime cost + factory overheads + opening WIP - closing WIP.
Cost of production adds quality control, process R&D, production administration and primary packing, less scrap recoveries.
Cost of sales = cost of goods sold + general administration + selling and distribution overheads.
High-low method: variable rate = change in cost / change in activity.
Fixed cost is constant in total, variable cost is constant per unit.
Profit of x% on price = x/(100 - x) on cost (20% on price = 25% on cost).

cases.title: Case: Sharma Auto Components
cases.body:
Sharma Auto Components makes a single brake assembly. Data for the year:

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Opening stock of raw material | 1,20,000 |
| Purchases of raw material | 8,40,000 |
| Carriage inward | 20,000 |
| Closing stock of raw material | 1,60,000 |
| Direct wages | 4,50,000 |
| Hire charges of special machine for this product | 30,000 |
| Factory overheads | 2,60,000 |
| Opening WIP | 70,000 |
| Closing WIP | 90,000 |
| Quality control cost | 25,000 |
| Research and development (production process) | 15,000 |
| Administration overheads relating to production | 40,000 |
| Primary packing | 20,000 |
| Sale of scrap | 10,000 |
| General administration overheads | 60,000 |
| Selling and distribution overheads (incl. secondary packing) | 1,10,000 |

Units produced: 10,000. Opening finished goods: 500 units valued at ₹75,000. Closing finished goods: 1,000 units, valued at the current year's cost of production per unit (FIFO). Selling price ₹200 per unit.

questions.explanation: Opening 1,20,000 + purchases 8,40,000 + carriage inward 20,000 - closing 1,60,000 = ₹8,20,000. Carriage inward is part of material cost.

questions.prompt: Where does the primary packing cost of ₹20,000 appear in the cost sheet?
questions.explanation: Primary packing is needed to make the product saleable, so it is added after works cost to arrive at cost of production. Secondary packing goes to selling and distribution.

| Less closing finished goods (1,000 x ₹163) | (1,63,000) |

questions.prompt: Compute the profit for the year. Round to the nearest rupee.
A hospital wants to know the cost of running its cardiology ward for a month. In costing terms, the ward is a:
questions.explanation: A cost object is anything whose cost is measured separately. The cost unit for the ward would be a patient-day; the ward itself is the object being costed.

questions.prompt: A company spent ₹2,00,000 last year on a feasibility study for a new plant. While deciding now whether to build the plant, this ₹2,00,000 is:
questions.explanation: It is already incurred and cannot be changed by the decision, so it is a sunk cost and is ignored in decision making.

questions.prompt: Which cost is semi-variable?
options: Electricity bill with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-unit charge
questions.explanation: A fixed demand charge plus a usage-based charge gives a cost that has both a fixed and a variable element.

questions.prompt: Within the relevant range, fixed cost per unit remains constant as output increases.
questions.explanation: Fixed cost is constant in total. Spread over more units, fixed cost per unit falls as output rises.

questions.prompt: Select the correct pairs of industry and cost unit.
questions.explanation: Brick making uses per 1,000 bricks as the cost unit. A labour hour is a measure of input, not a unit of output.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the benefit given up by choosing one alternative over the next best one is called ___ cost.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is not recorded in the books but is relevant for decisions, for example rent forgone by using an owned building.

questions.prompt: Using the high-low method, estimate total maintenance cost at 6,000 units. Round to the nearest rupee.
From last year's data, derive overhead recovery rates and prepare a statement showing the price to be quoted for a tender. The firm wants a profit of 20% on the selling price.
questions.data:
Last year: direct material ₹6,00,000, direct wages ₹4,00,000, works overheads ₹2,40,000, office overheads ₹1,24,000. Works overheads are recovered on direct wages; office overheads on works cost.

The tender needs material ₹50,000 and direct wages ₹30,000.
questions.answer:
Recovery rates: works overheads = 2,40,000 / 4,00,000 = **60% of direct wages**. Works cost last year = 6,00,000 + 4,00,000 + 2,40,000 = 12,40,000, so office overheads = 1,24,000 / 12,40,000 = **10% of works cost**.

| Statement of tender price | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Direct material | 50,000 |
| Direct wages | 30,000 |
| **Prime cost** | 80,000 |
| Works overheads (60% of 30,000) | 18,000 |
| **Works cost** | 98,000 |
| Office overheads (10% of 98,000) | 9,800 |
| **Cost of production** | 1,07,800 |
| Profit (25% on cost = 20% on price) | 26,950 |
| **Price to be quoted** | **1,34,750** |

Check: 26,950 / 1,34,750 = 20%.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between cost control and cost reduction.
questions.answer:
- **Cost control** keeps actual costs within set targets (standards, budgets). It accepts the standard as given and acts on variances.
- **Cost reduction** is a real and permanent fall in unit cost without hurting the product's quality or usefulness. It challenges the standards themselves.
- Control is preventive and works on the present; reduction is corrective and looks for new methods, designs and processes.
- Control ends once the target is met; reduction is continuous.
- Tools: control uses budgetary control and standard costing; reduction uses value analysis, work study, standardisation and process re-engineering.
- Temporary savings (for example, delaying maintenance) are not cost reduction.

questions.prompt: Explain the types of responsibility centres with an example of how each manager is evaluated.
questions.answer:
- **Cost centre**: manager controls costs only (a machining shop); judged on actual cost against budget or standard.
- **Revenue centre**: manager controls revenue (a regional sales office); judged on sales against target.
- **Profit centre**: manager controls both costs and revenue (a product division); judged on divisional profit.
- **Investment centre**: manager also controls capital employed (a subsidiary); judged on return on investment or residual income.
- The principle is that a manager should be held responsible only for items he can control (controllable costs), which supports goal congruence.

chapters.title: Material Cost
chapters.summary: Purchase and storage of material, EOQ, stock levels, pricing of issues, ABC analysis and treatment of material losses.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Cost of material purchased
lesson.body:
Material is recorded at the cost of bringing it to the factory in usable condition:

| Include | Exclude |
| --- | --- |
| Invoice price less trade discount and quantity discount | Cash discount (a finance item) |
| Duties and taxes for which input credit is not available | GST or other taxes for which input credit is available |
| Freight inward, insurance in transit, loading and unloading | Interest on money borrowed to buy material |
| Cost of containers (less credit for returnable containers) | Demurrage and penalties (abnormal, to costing P&L) |

Normal shortage in transit is absorbed by spreading the cost over the good units received; abnormal shortage is written off to the costing profit and loss account.

lesson.heading: EOQ and stock levels
lesson.body:
**Economic Order Quantity** balances ordering cost against carrying cost:

`EOQ = sqrt(2AO / C)`, where A = annual demand in units, O = cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year (often a % of unit price).

At EOQ, annual ordering cost equals annual carrying cost. When a supplier offers a **quantity discount**, compare the total annual cost (purchase + ordering + carrying) at EOQ and at each discount quantity; choose the lowest. Carrying cost at the discount quantity uses the discounted price.

Stock levels (use usage per period and lead time in the same period units):

| Level | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Re-order level (ROL) | Maximum usage x maximum lead time |
| Minimum level | ROL - (normal usage x normal lead time) |
| Maximum level | ROL + ROQ - (minimum usage x minimum lead time) |
| Average stock level | (Minimum + Maximum) / 2, or Minimum + ROQ / 2 |
| Danger level | Normal (or average) usage x lead time for emergency purchase |

Inventory turnover ratio = material consumed / average stock. A high ratio means fast-moving stock; a low ratio points to slow-moving or obsolete items.

lesson.heading: Pricing of issues and ABC analysis
lesson.body:
- **FIFO**: issues are priced at the oldest lots first. In rising prices, issues are cheaper and closing stock is near current prices, so profit is higher.
- **LIFO**: issues at latest prices; matches current cost with revenue but closing stock is undervalued. It is not allowed for financial statements but remains a costing method.
- **Weighted average**: a new average rate after every receipt = total value in stock / total quantity in stock.
- **Simple average**, **standard price** and **replacement price** are other methods.

Worked weighted average example: opening 200 units at ₹50, receipt of 300 at ₹55. New rate = 26,500 / 500 = ₹53. An issue of 350 units is priced at ₹18,550, leaving 150 units worth ₹7,950.

**ABC analysis** (always better control): A items are about 10% of items but about 70% of value, tightly controlled with frequent review and exact EOQ; B items get moderate control; C items (many items, little value) get simple rules such as bulk ordering. Other selective techniques: VED (vital, essential, desirable), FSN (fast, slow, non-moving), HML (high, medium, low price).

lesson.heading: Material losses and common mistakes
lesson.body:
| Loss | Normal | Abnormal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wastage (no value) | Absorbed by good units (raises unit cost) | Costing P&L |
| Scrap (small realisable value) | Sale value credited to the job, process or overheads | Costing P&L, net of realisable value |
| Spoilage (cannot be rectified) | Charged to production | Costing P&L |
| Defectives (can be rectified) | Rectification cost to the job or to overheads | Costing P&L |

Common mistakes:

- Taking annual carrying cost per unit as the full price instead of price x carrying %.
- Forgetting that the minimum level uses **normal** usage and **normal** lead time, while ROL uses **maximum** values.
- Not recomputing the weighted average rate after each receipt (only receipts change the rate, issues do not).
- Using the undiscounted price for carrying cost when evaluating a quantity discount.

keyPoints: EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C); at EOQ ordering cost = carrying cost.
ROL = maximum usage x maximum lead time.
Minimum = ROL - normal usage x normal lead time; Maximum = ROL + ROQ - minimum usage x minimum lead time.
Cash discount and recoverable taxes are excluded from material cost.
FIFO in rising prices gives lower cost of issues and higher profit.
Weighted average rate changes only on receipts.
ABC: A items, few in number and high in value, get the tightest control.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Pumps Ltd
cases.body:
Kaveri Pumps Ltd uses a casting, KP-7, in all its pumps. It works 48 weeks a year.

| Data | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Annual requirement | 24,000 units |
| Cost of placing one order | ₹1,200 |
| Purchase price | ₹100 per unit |
| Carrying cost | 10% of purchase price per year |
| Weekly usage (maximum / normal / minimum) | 650 / 500 / 350 units |
| Lead time (maximum / normal / minimum) | 6 / 5 / 4 weeks |

The supplier offers a 2% discount on the price if each order is for 6,000 units. The company currently orders the EOQ, and the re-order quantity in stock-level calculations is the EOQ.

questions.prompt: Compute the economic order quantity in units.
At the EOQ, how many orders are placed a year and what is the total of ordering and carrying cost?
questions.explanation: Orders = 24,000 / 2,400 = 10. Ordering cost = 10 x 1,200 = ₹12,000; carrying cost = 2,400/2 x 10 = ₹12,000. Total ₹24,000. The two are equal at EOQ.

questions.prompt: Should the company accept the 2% discount offer, and what is the annual effect?
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | At EOQ 2,400 | At 6,000 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purchase cost | 24,00,000 | 23,52,000 |
| Ordering cost | 12,000 | 4,800 (4 orders) |
| Carrying cost | 12,000 | 29,400 (3,000 x 9.80) |
| **Total** | 24,24,000 | 23,86,200 |

Accept: saving ₹37,800. Carrying cost rises by ₹17,400 but the price saving of ₹48,000 and ordering saving of ₹7,200 outweigh it.

questions.prompt: Compute the re-order level in units.
questions.explanation: ROL = maximum usage x maximum lead time = 650 x 6 = 3,900 units.

questions.prompt: Compute the maximum stock level in units.
questions.explanation: Maximum = ROL + ROQ - minimum usage x minimum lead time = 3,900 + 2,400 - 350 x 4 = 4,900 units. (Minimum level = 3,900 - 500 x 5 = 1,400; average = 3,150.)

questions.prompt: Under ABC analysis, 'A' category items are typically:
options: Large in number and low in value
Small in number and high in value
Vital for production regardless of value
questions.explanation: A items are a small share of the number of items but a large share of consumption value, so they get the closest control. Vital items are a VED classification.

questions.prompt: Material consumed during the year was ₹9,60,000. Opening stock was ₹1,40,000 and closing stock ₹1,80,000. What are the inventory turnover ratio and the average days of stock holding (360-day year)?
When prices are rising, FIFO gives a lower cost of materials issued and a higher profit than LIFO.
questions.explanation: FIFO charges the older, cheaper lots to production first, so cost of issues is lower and profit higher. Closing stock carries the newer, higher prices.

questions.prompt: Which items are included in the cost of material purchased?
options: GST for which input tax credit is available
Interest on loan taken to buy material
questions.explanation: Freight inward and non-creditable duty are added; trade discount is deducted. Recoverable GST, cash discount and interest are not part of material cost.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the stock level at which a fresh purchase order is placed is called the ___ level.
questions.explanation: Re-order level = maximum usage x maximum lead time, so stock does not run out even in the worst case before the new lot arrives.

questions.prompt: What is ABC analysis? State its advantages.
questions.answer:
- ABC analysis classifies stock items by annual consumption value: A (about 10% of items, 70% of value), B (about 20% / 20%), C (about 70% / 10%). The exact cut-offs are set by the firm.
- It is called "always better control" because control effort follows value.
- A items: strict control, exact EOQ, frequent review, close follow-up, low safety stock.
- C items: simple rules, bulk ordering, larger safety stock.
- Advantages: lower investment in inventory, less clerical effort on low-value items, better use of managerial time, fewer stock-outs of costly items.
- Limitation: it ignores criticality, so it is often combined with VED or FSN analysis.

questions.prompt: Explain the treatment of normal and abnormal wastage, scrap, spoilage and defectives in cost accounts.
questions.answer:
- **Wastage**: normal wastage is absorbed by good units, raising unit cost; abnormal wastage is valued like good units and charged to costing P&L.
- **Scrap**: if value is small, sale proceeds are credited to overheads or the costing P&L; if identifiable with a job or process, credited to that job or process; abnormal scrap goes to costing P&L net of realisable value.
- **Spoilage**: normal spoilage cost is included in production cost (or overheads); abnormal spoilage goes to costing P&L.
- **Defectives**: rectification cost of normal defectives is charged to the job (if identifiable) or to overheads; abnormal defectives go to costing P&L.
- The principle is that normal losses are part of the cost of good output, abnormal losses are not.

chapters.title: Employee Cost and Direct Expenses
chapters.summary: Recording and costing labour, idle time and overtime, labour turnover, time and piece incentive plans (Halsey, Rowan, differential piece rates) and direct expenses.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Components and control of employee cost
lesson.body:
Employee cost includes wages and salaries, overtime and bonus, the employer's contribution to provident fund and ESI, gratuity and leave encashment, and other benefits. Direct employee cost is traceable to a cost object (a machinist's time on a job); the rest is indirect and goes to overheads.

Departments involved: HR (recruitment and records), engineering and work study (job analysis, standards), timekeeping (attendance), time booking (time spent on each job), and payroll.

**Idle time** is time paid for but not worked:

- Normal idle time (tea breaks, tool setting, waiting between jobs) is part of the cost of production; it is spread by inflating the hourly rate or charged to factory overheads.
- Abnormal idle time (power failure, strike, machine breakdown) is charged to the costing profit and loss account.

**Overtime premium** (the extra over the normal rate):

- Done at a customer's request: charge to that job.
- Done because of general pressure of work: charge to production overheads.
- Due to abnormal reasons (fire, flood): costing P&L.

lesson.heading: Labour turnover
lesson.body:
Labour turnover is the rate of change in the workforce. Average workers = (opening + closing) / 2.

| Method | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Separation | Separations / average workers x 100 |
| Replacement | Replacements / average workers x 100 |
| Flux | (Separations + replacements) / average workers x 100 |
| Flux including new accessions | (Separations + accessions) / average workers x 100, where accessions = replacements + new recruits for expansion |

Replacement method counts only those recruited to fill vacancies, not new posts created by expansion.

Costs of labour turnover: **preventive costs** (welfare, personnel administration, medical, better pay) and **replacement costs** (recruitment, selection, training, loss of output and higher scrap while new workers learn, extra tool breakage).

lesson.heading: Incentive plans
lesson.body:
Let S = standard time, T = time taken, R = hourly rate.

| Plan | Earnings |
| --- | --- |
| Time rate | T x R |
| Straight piece rate | Units x piece rate |
| Halsey | T x R + 50% x (S - T) x R |
| Halsey-Weir | T x R + 30% x (S - T) x R |
| Rowan | T x R + ((S - T) / S) x T x R |
| Differential piece rate | Lower rate below standard output, higher rate at or above standard (rates as stated in the question) |

Halsey and Rowan both guarantee time wages. Rowan gives higher earnings than Halsey when time saved is less than 50% of standard time; both give the same at exactly 50%; Halsey is higher above 50%. Under Rowan the bonus can never exceed the time wages for the hours worked, which protects the employer against loose standards.

Taylor's differential piece rate pays a low piece rate (commonly 83% of the normal rate) below standard efficiency and a high rate (commonly 125%) at or above it. Merrick's multiple piece rate adds a middle step. Always use the percentages given in the question.

lesson.heading: Worked example, direct expenses and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Standard time 12 hours, rate ₹150, time taken 9 hours:

- Halsey = 9 x 150 + 0.5 x 3 x 150 = 1,350 + 225 = ₹1,575
- Rowan = 1,350 + (3/12) x 9 x 150 = 1,350 + 337.50 = ₹1,687.50

**Direct expenses** are costs other than material and employee cost that can be traced to a cost object: hire of special plant for a job, royalty based on units produced, cost of special designs or patterns, sub-contract (job work) charges, and travelling expenses for a specific job. If small, they may be treated as overheads.

Common mistakes:

- Applying Rowan's ratio to standard time instead of time taken.
- Counting new recruits for expansion as replacements.
- Charging all overtime premium to the job instead of following the reason.
- Treating abnormal idle time as overheads.

keyPoints: Halsey bonus = 50% x time saved x rate.
Rowan bonus = (time saved / time allowed) x time taken x rate.
Halsey and Rowan earnings are equal when time taken is half the time allowed.
Replacement method: replacements / average workers x 100; flux = (separations + replacements) / average x 100.
Normal idle time is a production cost; abnormal idle time goes to costing P&L.
Overtime premium: customer request to the job, general pressure to overheads, abnormal to costing P&L.

cases.title: Case: Ramesh and Suresh at Precision Tools
cases.body: Precision Tools pays ₹150 an hour. The standard time for a die-setting job is 12 hours. In one week Ramesh completes the job in 9 hours and Suresh in 10 hours. Management is choosing between the Halsey plan (50% bonus) and the Rowan plan.

questions.prompt: Compute Ramesh's earnings for the job under the Halsey plan. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation: Time wages 9 x 150 = 1,350. Bonus = 50% x (12 - 9) x 150 = 225. Earnings = ₹1,575.

questions.prompt: Compute Ramesh's earnings for the job under the Rowan plan, to 2 decimals.
Compute Suresh's effective hourly earning rate under the Rowan plan, to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Rowan earnings = 10 x 150 + (2/12) x 10 x 150 = 1,500 + 250 = ₹1,750. Effective rate = 1,750 / 10 = ₹175.00 per hour.

questions.prompt: At what time taken for this job would a worker earn the same amount under Halsey and Rowan?
questions.explanation: Equal when 0.5 x (S - T) = (S - T) x T / S, that is T = S / 2 = 6 hours. Check: both give 6 x 150 + 450 = ₹1,350.

questions.prompt: For both Ramesh and Suresh, which plan pays more, and why?
options: Rowan, because time saved is less than 50% of the standard time
Halsey, because the bonus share is fixed at 50%
Halsey, because time saved is more than 50%
questions.explanation: Time saved is 25% (Ramesh) and 16.7% (Suresh) of standard. Below 50% time saved, Rowan pays more than Halsey.

questions.prompt: Compute the labour turnover rate under the replacement method, as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.data: Workers on roll: 1 April 1,800; 31 March 2,200. During the year 120 workers left, 90 were recruited to fill those vacancies and 300 were recruited for a new expansion line.
questions.explanation: Average workers = (1,800 + 2,200) / 2 = 2,000. Replacement rate = 90 / 2,000 x 100 = 4.50%. The 300 expansion recruits are not replacements.

questions.prompt: Using the same data (average workers 2,000; separations 120; replacements 90; new recruits for expansion 300), what is the labour turnover under the flux method based on separations and replacements?
questions.explanation: Flux = (120 + 90) / 2,000 x 100 = 10.50%. Including all accessions (90 + 300) it would be 25.50%; separation method gives 6.00%.

questions.prompt: Workers worked overtime because the factory as a whole had more orders than normal capacity. The overtime premium should be:
options: Charged to the jobs done during overtime hours
Charged to costing profit and loss
questions.explanation: When overtime results from general pressure of work, it is not fair to load the jobs that happen to fall in overtime hours. The premium is spread through production overheads.

questions.prompt: Idle time caused by a power breakdown lasting three days is charged to the costing profit and loss account.
questions.explanation: A long power breakdown is abnormal idle time. It is not a cost of normal production, so it is written off to costing P&L.

questions.prompt: Which of these are direct expenses?
options: Hire charges of a crane used only for one contract
Cost of special drawings for a specific job
questions.explanation: Hire of special plant, royalty on production and job-specific designs are traceable to the cost object. Factory rent and the works manager's salary are indirect (factory overheads).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under the ___ plan the bonus is the proportion of time saved to time allowed, applied to time-wages for the time taken.
questions.explanation: Rowan bonus = (time saved / time allowed) x time taken x rate.

questions.prompt: Compute the daily earnings of each worker under (a) the differential piece rate scheme and (b) time rate, and comment.
questions.data:
Standard output: 40 units per 8-hour day. Normal piece rate ₹20 per unit. Differential scheme: 80% of the piece rate below standard output, 120% of the piece rate at or above standard. Time rate ₹60 per hour.

| Worker | Output in the day |
| --- | --- |
| Anil | 32 units |
| Bina | 40 units |
| Chetan | 45 units |
questions.answer:
| Worker | Output | Efficiency | Piece rate applied (₹) | Differential earnings (₹) | Time rate earnings (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anil | 32 | 80.0% | 16 | 512 | 480 |
| Bina | 40 | 100.0% | 24 | 960 | 480 |
| Chetan | 45 | 112.5% | 24 | 1,080 | 480 |

Comment: Anil (80% efficient) earns less than time wages, which penalises the inefficient worker. Bina at standard earns twice her time wage. Chetan earns ₹1,080. The scheme rewards reaching the standard sharply, so the standard must be set by proper work study, and the scheme is usually combined with a guaranteed minimum wage required by law.

questions.prompt: Explain the causes of labour turnover and the costs associated with it.
questions.answer:
- **Personal causes**: better job elsewhere, family reasons, ill health, marriage, retirement.
- **Unavoidable causes**: seasonal work, shortage of material or orders, disciplinary dismissal, retrenchment.
- **Avoidable causes**: low pay, poor working conditions, lack of promotion, bad relations with supervisors, unsuitable job.
- **Preventive costs** are incurred to keep turnover low: personnel department, welfare, medical services, pension and incentive schemes.
- **Replacement costs** arise when workers leave: recruitment and selection, training, loss of output during learning, more scrap and defective work, extra tool breakage.
- Turnover is measured by the separation, replacement and flux methods and reported to management with an analysis of causes.

questions.prompt: How are idle time and overtime premium treated in cost accounts?
questions.answer:
- **Normal idle time** is unavoidable (breaks, set-ups, waiting for work). It is part of the cost of production: either the hourly rate is inflated to cover it, or it is charged to factory overheads.
- **Abnormal idle time** (strikes, lockouts, long breakdowns, power failure) is charged to costing P&L, so that product costs are not distorted.
- **Overtime premium** at a customer's request is charged to the job; due to general pressure of work, to production overheads; due to abnormal events, to costing P&L.
- The normal-rate portion of overtime hours is charged to the job as ordinary wages.
- Regular reports of idle time and overtime by cause help management control them.

chapters.title: Overheads: Absorption Costing
chapters.summary: Collection, allocation and apportionment of overheads, secondary distribution of service departments, absorption rates including the machine hour rate, and under or over absorption.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Allocation and primary distribution
lesson.body:
Overheads are indirect costs: indirect material, indirect employee cost and indirect expenses. They are classified by function (production, administration, selling, distribution) and by behaviour (fixed, variable, semi-variable).

- **Allocation**: charging a whole item of cost to one cost centre because it was incurred only for that centre (salary of the machine shop foreman to the machine shop).
- **Apportionment**: sharing a common cost among centres on a fair basis.

| Overhead | Basis of apportionment |
| --- | --- |
| Rent, rates, building insurance, lighting (if no meters) | Floor area |
| Power | Horse power x machine hours (or kWh) |
| Depreciation, insurance of plant | Capital value of plant |
| Canteen, welfare, personnel department | Number of employees |
| Supervision | Number of employees or direct wages |
| Lighting | Number of light points |

The result is the **primary distribution summary**: total overheads of each production and service department.

lesson.heading: Secondary distribution
lesson.body:
Service department totals are then re-apportioned to production departments:

- **Direct redistribution**: service costs go only to production departments; services between service departments are ignored.
- **Step method (non-reciprocal)**: service departments are closed one by one, usually starting with the one serving the most departments; a closed department receives nothing back.
- **Reciprocal methods**: recognise mutual services fully. Three ways: simultaneous equations, repeated distribution, and trial and error.

Simultaneous equations: if service X gets 20% of Y's cost and Y gets 20% of X's:

`X = own cost of X + 0.2Y` and `Y = own cost of Y + 0.2X`

Solve for the total X and Y, then share each total among all departments in the given percentages. The final totals of production departments must equal the total of all overheads before secondary distribution: use this as a check.

lesson.heading: Absorption and the machine hour rate
lesson.body:
Absorption charges overheads to cost units with a predetermined rate = budgeted overheads / budgeted base. Bases: % of direct material, % of prime cost, % of direct wages, rate per direct labour hour, rate per machine hour, rate per unit.

Use the machine hour rate where machines do most of the work. Compute it on effective running hours:

| Machine hour rate (worked example) | ₹ per hour |
| --- | --- |
| Standing charges: rent 36,000 + supervision 54,000 + insurance 18,000 = 1,08,000 / 1,800 hrs | 60.00 |
| Depreciation (12,00,000 - 1,20,000) / 10 years = 1,08,000 / 1,800 hrs | 60.00 |
| Power: 15 units per hour x ₹8 | 120.00 |
| Repairs 36,000 / 1,800 hrs | 20.00 |
| **Machine hour rate** | **260.00** |

A **blanket (single plant-wide) rate** is simple but distorts product costs when products use departments differently. **Departmental rates** are more accurate.

lesson.heading: Under and over absorption
lesson.body:
Absorbed overheads = actual base x predetermined rate. If absorbed is less than actual overheads, the difference is **under-absorbed**; if more, **over-absorbed**.

Causes: error in estimating overheads or activity, unforeseen changes in prices, idle capacity, seasonal swings, change in methods.

Treatment:

- Small amounts: write off to costing P&L.
- Large amounts due to wrong estimates: **supplementary rate** spread over work-in-progress, finished goods and cost of sales (in proportion to the overheads already absorbed in them, or to equivalent units).
- Due to abnormal factors (idle capacity, strike): costing P&L.
- Seasonal businesses: carry forward to the next period within the year.

Common mistakes: using actual overheads / actual hours as the absorption rate; adding the closed service department back in the step method; forgetting that the two production totals must add to the grand total.

keyPoints: Allocation charges a whole cost to one centre; apportionment shares a common cost.
Rent on floor area, power on HP x machine hours, depreciation on asset value, canteen on employees.
Reciprocal method: solve X = a + pY, Y = b + qX, then distribute totals.
Machine hour rate = (standing charges + machine expenses) / effective running hours.
Under-absorbed = actual overheads - absorbed overheads.
Large under/over absorption from wrong estimates: supplementary rate over WIP, FG and cost of sales.

cases.title: Case: Deccan Castings
cases.body:
Deccan Castings has two production departments (P1 machining, P2 assembly) and two service departments (S1 maintenance, S2 stores). The primary distribution summary for the year shows:

| Department | P1 | P2 | S1 | S2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overheads (₹) | 4,80,000 | 3,60,000 | 1,20,000 | 90,000 |

Services are used as follows:

| Service department | P1 | P2 | S1 | S2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | 40% | 40% | - | 20% |
| S2 | 50% | 30% | 20% | - |

The company uses the reciprocal (simultaneous equation) method. P1 absorbs overheads on machine hours; budgeted machine hours of P1 are 25,000. Actual P1 overheads turned out to be ₹6,10,000 for 26,000 actual machine hours.

questions.prompt: Compute the total cost of S1 (maintenance) to be distributed under the simultaneous equation method. Round to the nearest rupee.
Compute the total overheads of P1 after secondary distribution. Round to the nearest rupee.
Compute P1's machine hour rate, to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: MHR = 5,96,875 / 25,000 hours = ₹23.875 = ₹23.88 per machine hour.

questions.prompt: Using the unrounded machine hour rate, what is P1's under or over absorption for the year?
questions.explanation: Absorbed = 26,000 x 23.875 = ₹6,20,750. Actual ₹6,10,000. Absorbed exceeds actual, so over-absorbed by ₹10,750.

questions.prompt: If Deccan used direct redistribution instead, what would change?
options: The 20% services exchanged between S1 and S2 would be ignored
P1 and P2 would get more than ₹10,50,000 in total
S1 would be closed first and receive nothing from S2
Service department costs would stay in S1 and S2
questions.explanation: Direct redistribution ignores inter-service work and shares each service department only between production departments (S1 in 40:40, S2 in 50:30). The total charged to production stays ₹10,50,000; only the split changes.

questions.prompt: The most appropriate basis for apportioning power cost among production departments is:
questions.explanation: Power consumption depends on the rated power of machines and how long they run, so HP x machine hours (or metered kWh) is used.

questions.prompt: A single overhead rate for the whole factory (blanket rate) is suitable when:
options: Products pass through all departments and spend similar time in each
Departments have very different overhead rates
Some products use only one department
Machines and manual work are mixed differently for each product
questions.explanation: A blanket rate gives fair costs only when every product uses departments in the same proportion. Otherwise departmental rates are needed.

questions.prompt: Production overheads under-absorbed for the year are ₹1,20,000 and arise from an error in estimating the overhead rate. Using a supplementary rate based on equivalent units, how much should be charged to cost of sales? Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.data:
| Where the units are | Equivalent units |
| --- | --- |
| Work-in-progress | 2,000 |
| Finished goods | 3,000 |
| Cost of sales | 15,000 |
questions.explanation: Supplementary rate = 1,20,000 / (2,000 + 3,000 + 15,000) = ₹6 per unit. Cost of sales = 15,000 x 6 = ₹90,000; WIP ₹12,000; finished goods ₹18,000.

questions.prompt: Under-absorption caused by idle capacity due to a long strike should be charged to the costing profit and loss account, not spread over production.
questions.explanation: It is an abnormal cause. Spreading it over units would overstate their cost and stock values.

questions.prompt: Which of these can cause under or over absorption of overheads?
options: Actual overheads differ from budgeted overheads
Actual machine hours differ from budgeted hours
Allocating the foreman's salary to his own department
questions.explanation: Under or over absorption arises because a predetermined rate is applied to actual activity while actual costs differ. Allocating a cost to the right department does not by itself cause it.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: charging a whole item of overhead to one cost centre, because it was incurred wholly for that centre, is called ___.
questions.explanation: Allocation needs no basis because the cost belongs entirely to one centre. Apportionment shares common costs on a basis.

questions.prompt: Compute the machine hour rate for machine M-4.
questions.data: Cost of machine ₹12,00,000; estimated scrap value ₹1,20,000; life 10 years (straight line). Effective running time 1,800 hours a year. The machine's share of: rent ₹36,000, supervision ₹54,000 and insurance ₹18,000 a year. Power: 15 units an hour at ₹8 per unit. Repairs and maintenance ₹36,000 a year.
questions.answer:
| Particulars | Per year (₹) | Per hour (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Standing charges** |  |  |
| Rent | 36,000 |  |
| Supervision | 54,000 |  |
| Insurance | 18,000 |  |
| Total standing charges / 1,800 | 1,08,000 | 60.00 |
| **Machine expenses** |  |  |
| Depreciation (12,00,000 - 1,20,000) / 10 | 1,08,000 | 60.00 |
| Power (15 x ₹8) |  | 120.00 |
| Repairs and maintenance | 36,000 | 20.00 |
| **Machine hour rate** |  | **260.00** |

Standing charges accrue with time whatever the running hours, so they are spread over the effective hours. Running hours exclude maintenance and set-up time unless set-up is productive.

questions.prompt: What is under and over absorption of overheads? State its causes and accounting treatment.
questions.answer:
- Overheads are absorbed using a predetermined rate. Absorbed = actual base x rate. The difference from actual overheads is under-absorption (absorbed less than actual) or over-absorption.
- **Causes**: wrong estimate of overheads or activity level, price changes, idle capacity, seasonal variation, changes in production methods.
- **Treatment**: small amounts are written off to costing P&L; large amounts due to wrong estimates are adjusted through a supplementary rate across WIP, finished goods and cost of sales; amounts due to abnormal causes go to costing P&L; in seasonal businesses they may be carried forward within the year.
- A supplementary rate may be positive (under-absorbed) or negative (over-absorbed).

questions.prompt: Distinguish between allocation and apportionment of overheads.
questions.answer:
- **Allocation** charges a whole item of cost to a cost centre because it is identifiable with that centre (depreciation of a machine in one department).
- **Apportionment** shares an item common to several centres on a suitable basis (factory rent on floor area).
- Allocation needs no basis; apportionment depends on a basis reflecting benefit received.
- Allocation is direct and exact; apportionment involves judgement and can be arbitrary.
- Both are part of primary distribution; secondary distribution then apportions service department costs to production departments.

chapters.title: Activity Based Costing
chapters.summary: Tracing overheads to products through activities and cost drivers, the cost hierarchy, comparison with traditional absorption, and activity based management.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Why ABC
lesson.body:
Traditional absorption spreads all production overheads on one volume base such as labour or machine hours. That works when overheads are small and driven by volume. In modern plants many overheads are driven by **activities** that have nothing to do with volume: set-ups, purchase orders, inspections, engineering changes.

The result is **cross-subsidisation**: high-volume, simple products are overcosted and low-volume, complex products are undercosted. Pricing and product-mix decisions then go wrong.

**Activity Based Costing** first assigns overheads to activities (cost pools) and then to products in proportion to their use of each activity, measured by a **cost driver**.

lesson.heading: Steps and the cost hierarchy
lesson.body:
Steps:

- Identify the main activities.
- Collect overheads into an activity cost pool for each activity.
- Choose a cost driver for each pool (what makes the cost change).
- Activity rate = cost of pool / total driver volume.
- Charge each product: activity rate x driver units it uses.

| Level | Cost varies with | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit level | Each unit produced | Machine power, direct material handling per unit |
| Batch level | Each batch | Set-ups, purchase orders, batch inspection, material moves |
| Product (service) sustaining | Each product line | Product design, engineering changes, maintaining specifications |
| Facility sustaining | Running the plant as a whole | Factory rent, plant manager's salary, security |

Facility-sustaining costs have no product-related driver; they are often apportioned arbitrarily or kept out of product costs.

lesson.heading: Worked example
lesson.body:
A firm makes 10,000 Standard and 2,000 Deluxe units, each taking 2 labour hours. Overheads ₹12,00,000 are absorbed traditionally at ₹50 per labour hour, so ₹100 per unit for both.

| Activity | Cost (₹) | Driver: Standard / Deluxe | Rate (₹) | Standard (₹) | Deluxe (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Machine set-ups | 4,80,000 | 20 / 60 | 6,000 | 1,20,000 | 3,60,000 |
| Purchase orders | 3,00,000 | 100 / 200 | 1,000 | 1,00,000 | 2,00,000 |
| Quality inspections | 4,20,000 | 50 / 90 | 3,000 | 1,50,000 | 2,70,000 |
| **Total** | 12,00,000 |  |  | 3,70,000 | 8,30,000 |
| **Per unit** |  |  |  | 37 | 415 |

Traditional costing charged Deluxe ₹100 instead of ₹415 a unit, undercosting it by ₹315, while Standard was overcosted by ₹63.

lesson.heading: Activity based management and common mistakes
lesson.body:
ABC data supports **activity based management (ABM)**:

- **Value-added activities** increase what the customer will pay for (machining, assembly).
- **Non-value-added activities** add cost but no value (moving material, waiting, storage, rework, excess inspection). ABM tries to reduce or remove them.
- Cost driver analysis, activity analysis and performance measures follow from ABC.

ABC suits firms with high overheads, diverse products, varied batch sizes and complex processes. It is costly to set up and keep current, and choosing drivers involves judgement.

Common mistakes:

- Dividing an activity cost by units produced instead of by the driver volume.
- Forgetting that total overheads stay the same under both methods; only the split changes. Check that product totals add up.
- Calling set-up cost a unit-level cost: it is batch level.

keyPoints: Activity rate = activity cost pool / total cost driver volume.
Product overhead = sum of (activity rate x driver units used).
Hierarchy: unit, batch, product-sustaining, facility-sustaining.
Traditional absorption overcosts high-volume simple products and undercosts low-volume complex ones.
Total overheads are the same under both methods; only allocation between products changes.
ABM targets non-value-added activities.

cases.title: Case: Nirmal Appliances
cases.body:
Nirmal Appliances makes two mixers: Standard (10,000 units) and Deluxe (2,000 units). Each unit takes 2 direct labour hours. Production overheads of ₹12,00,000 are currently absorbed on direct labour hours. A consultant has analysed the overheads:

| Activity | Cost (₹) | Cost driver | Standard | Deluxe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Machine set-ups | 4,80,000 | Number of set-ups | 20 | 60 |
| Purchase orders | 3,00,000 | Number of purchase orders | 100 | 200 |
| Quality inspections | 4,20,000 | Number of inspections | 50 | 90 |

questions.prompt: Compute the cost per machine set-up.
questions.explanation: Set-up cost ₹4,80,000 / (20 + 60) set-ups = ₹6,000 per set-up.

questions.prompt: Compute the overhead cost per unit of Deluxe under ABC, to 2 decimals.
Compute the overhead cost per unit of Standard under ABC, to 2 decimals.
Compared with ABC, how does the current labour-hour method treat Deluxe?
options: Costs it correctly because both take 2 hours
questions.explanation: Traditional rate = 12,00,000 / 24,000 hours = ₹50 per hour, so ₹100 per unit. ABC gives ₹415. Deluxe is undercosted by ₹315 a unit; Standard is overcosted by ₹63 (100 - 37).

questions.prompt: In the cost hierarchy, machine set-up cost at Nirmal is a:
questions.explanation: A set-up is done once per batch whatever the batch size, so its cost varies with the number of batches.

questions.prompt: The most suitable cost driver for the cost of the purchasing department is:
questions.explanation: Purchasing effort depends on how many orders are raised, not on their value or on output volume.

questions.prompt: Which is a facility-sustaining activity?
options: Running a machine for each unit
questions.explanation: Security and plant management support the whole plant and cannot be linked to units, batches or products.

questions.prompt: ABC gives the greatest benefit when overheads are a small part of total cost and all products are made in similar batch sizes.
questions.explanation: ABC adds most value when overheads are high, products are diverse and batch sizes and complexity vary. Otherwise traditional absorption gives similar results at lower cost.

questions.prompt: Which activities are non-value-added?
options: Moving material between stores and shop floor
Storing finished goods for long periods
questions.explanation: Moving, rework and storage add cost but nothing the customer pays for. Machining and assembly change the product and add value.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the factor that causes the cost of an activity to change, used to charge that activity to products, is called a cost ___.
questions.explanation: Examples: number of set-ups, purchase orders, inspections, material moves.

questions.prompt: Compute the total cost of customer order 47 under ABC. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.data: Material handling cost ₹2,40,000 for 1,200 moves a year. Set-up cost ₹1,50,000 for 300 set-ups a year. Order 47 uses direct material and labour of ₹18,000, needs 15 material moves and 4 set-ups.

questions.prompt: Compute the unit cost and unit profit of Alpha and Beta under (a) traditional absorption on machine hours and (b) ABC. Comment on the result.
questions.data:
| Product | Units | Price (₹) | Direct material (₹/unit) | Direct labour (₹/unit) | Machine hours per unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alpha | 5,000 | 300 | 120 | 60 | 1 |
| Beta | 1,000 | 400 | 150 | 80 | 2 |

Production overheads ₹7,00,000:

| Activity | Cost (₹) | Driver | Alpha | Beta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Machining | 2,80,000 | machine hours | 5,000 | 2,000 |
| Set-ups | 2,40,000 | set-ups | 10 | 30 |
| Despatch | 1,80,000 | despatches | 60 | 60 |
questions.answer:
**(a) Traditional**: total machine hours = 5,000 x 1 + 1,000 x 2 = 7,000. Rate = 7,00,000 / 7,000 = ₹100 per machine hour.

**(b) ABC rates**: machining 2,80,000 / 7,000 = ₹40 per hour; set-ups 2,40,000 / 40 = ₹6,000; despatch 1,80,000 / 120 = ₹1,500.

| ABC overheads | Alpha (₹) | Beta (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Machining | 2,00,000 | 80,000 |
| Set-ups | 60,000 | 1,80,000 |
| Despatch | 90,000 | 90,000 |
| **Total** | 3,50,000 | 3,50,000 |
| **Per unit** | 70 | 350 |

| Per unit (₹) | Alpha: traditional | Alpha: ABC | Beta: traditional | Beta: ABC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct material | 120 | 120 | 150 | 150 |
| Direct labour | 60 | 60 | 80 | 80 |
| Overheads | 100 | 70 | 200 | 350 |
| **Total cost** | 280 | 250 | 430 | 580 |
| Price | 300 | 300 | 400 | 400 |
| **Profit / (loss)** | 20 | 50 | (30) | (180) |

Comment: total profit is the same (₹70,000) under both methods. ABC shows Beta, the low-volume product with many set-ups, loses ₹180 a unit, not ₹30. Alpha was subsidising Beta. Management should review Beta's price, batch sizes and set-up frequency.

questions.prompt: Explain the cost hierarchy used in activity based costing with examples.
questions.answer:
- **Unit-level activities** are performed for each unit: machine running cost, power, unit-level inspection. Cost varies with output volume.
- **Batch-level activities** are performed for each batch: set-ups, purchase orders, material moves, first-piece inspection. Cost varies with number of batches, not units.
- **Product-sustaining activities** support a product line: product design, engineering changes, maintaining bills of material, advertising a specific product.
- **Facility-sustaining activities** support the plant as a whole: factory rent, plant manager's salary, security. They are not driven by products and are often kept out of product costs or apportioned.
- Traditional costing treats all overheads as unit level, which is the source of cost distortion.

questions.prompt: State the benefits and limitations of activity based costing.
questions.answer:
Benefits:

- More accurate product costs, removing cross-subsidisation between high and low volume products.
- Better pricing, product mix and make-or-buy decisions.
- Shows cost drivers, so managers can control costs by managing activities (ABM).
- Identifies non-value-added activities for elimination.
- Useful for customer and channel profitability.

Limitations:

- Costly and time-consuming to design and maintain.
- Choice of activities and drivers needs judgement; some costs (facility-sustaining) are still apportioned arbitrarily.
- Less useful where overheads are small or products are similar.
- Staff may resist the change from familiar methods.

chapters.title: Cost Accounting Systems
chapters.summary: Non-integrated (cost ledger) and integrated accounting systems, control accounts and journal entries, and reconciliation of cost and financial profit.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Non-integrated system: control accounts
lesson.body:
Under a **non-integrated (interlocking) system** the cost department keeps its own ledger. It records only cost items. Transactions with the outside world (creditors, debtors, bank) are posted to one account that stands for the financial ledger: the **Cost Ledger Control Account** (also called General Ledger Adjustment Account).

Main accounts in the cost ledger:

- Cost Ledger Control A/c
- Stores Ledger Control A/c
- Work-in-Progress (WIP) Control A/c
- Wages Control A/c
- Factory (Production) Overhead Control A/c, Administration Overhead Control A/c, Selling and Distribution Overhead Control A/c
- Finished Goods Control A/c
- Cost of Sales A/c and Costing Profit and Loss A/c

lesson.heading: Journal entries in the cost ledger
lesson.body:
| Transaction | Debit | Credit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material purchased | Stores Ledger Control | Cost Ledger Control |
| Direct material issued | WIP Control | Stores Ledger Control |
| Indirect material issued | Factory Overhead Control | Stores Ledger Control |
| Wages paid | Wages Control | Cost Ledger Control |
| Direct wages charged | WIP Control | Wages Control |
| Indirect wages charged | Factory Overhead Control | Wages Control |
| Overheads incurred (rent, power) | Factory Overhead Control | Cost Ledger Control |
| Factory overheads absorbed | WIP Control | Factory Overhead Control |
| Finished goods completed | Finished Goods Control | WIP Control |
| Cost of goods sold | Cost of Sales | Finished Goods Control |
| Sales | Cost Ledger Control | Costing P&L |
| Under-absorbed overheads written off | Costing P&L | Factory Overhead Control |

The balance on the Overhead Control account after absorption is the under (debit balance) or over (credit balance) absorption.

lesson.heading: Integrated accounting
lesson.body:
Under an **integrated system** one set of books serves both cost and financial purposes. Control accounts for stores, WIP, finished goods and overheads are kept in the main ledger along with debtors, creditors and bank. There is no Cost Ledger Control account; the real accounts are used directly (for example, Stores Ledger Control Dr, To Creditors).

Advantages: no duplication of work, no reconciliation needed, faster and consistent information, lower cost. Prerequisites: management decision on the extent of integration (up to prime cost or full integration), a suitable coding system, an agreed routine for documents, and perpetual inventory.

lesson.heading: Reconciliation of cost and financial profit
lesson.body:
In a non-integrated system the two profits differ. Reasons:

- **Items only in financial accounts**: interest, dividends and rent received; profit or loss on sale of assets; fines and penalties; preliminary expenses or goodwill written off; donations; income tax and appropriations.
- **Items only in cost accounts**: notional rent on own premises, notional interest on capital.
- **Under or over absorption** of overheads in cost accounts.
- **Different stock valuation** and **different depreciation** methods.

Memorandum reconciliation, starting from costing profit:

| Add to costing profit | Deduct from costing profit |
| --- | --- |
| Overheads over-absorbed in cost accounts | Overheads under-absorbed in cost accounts |
| Incomes only in financial accounts | Expenses only in financial accounts |
| Notional expenses only in cost accounts | Higher depreciation in financial accounts |
| Closing stock higher in financial accounts | Closing stock higher in cost accounts |
| Opening stock lower in financial accounts | Opening stock higher in financial accounts |

Test each item with one question: does it make financial profit higher or lower than costing profit? Higher means add. Common mistake: reversing the opening stock effect. A higher opening stock **reduces** profit.

keyPoints: Non-integrated: all external items go through Cost Ledger Control A/c.
Direct material and direct wages are debited to WIP Control; indirect ones to Overhead Control.
Overheads absorbed: WIP Control Dr, Factory Overhead Control Cr.
Debit balance on Overhead Control after absorption = under-absorbed.
Integrated accounts remove the need for reconciliation.
Starting from costing profit: add over-absorption, financial-only incomes and notional costs; deduct the opposites.

cases.title: Case: Ganga Textiles reconciliation
cases.body:
Ganga Textiles keeps separate cost and financial books. The cost accounts show a profit of ₹4,20,000 for the year. Differences found:

| Item | Details |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Factory overheads under-absorbed in cost accounts: ₹18,000 |
| 2 | Administration overheads over-absorbed in cost accounts: ₹12,000 |
| 3 | Depreciation charged: financial accounts ₹75,000, cost accounts ₹60,000 |
| 4 | Interest received on investments (not in cost accounts): ₹35,000 |
| 5 | Notional rent of own premises charged in cost accounts: ₹36,000 |
| 6 | Loss on sale of old machinery (not in cost accounts): ₹20,000 |
| 7 | Closing stock: cost accounts ₹1,40,000, financial accounts ₹1,30,000 |
| 8 | Opening stock: cost accounts ₹90,000, financial accounts ₹1,00,000 |

questions.prompt: Compute the profit as per financial accounts. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Item | Add (₹) | Less (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profit as per cost accounts | 4,20,000 |  |
| Factory overheads under-absorbed in cost accounts |  | 18,000 |
| Administration overheads over-absorbed in cost accounts | 12,000 |  |
| Depreciation charged: financial accounts ₹75,000, cost accounts ₹60,000 |  | 15,000 |
| Interest received on investments (not in cost accounts) | 35,000 |  |
| Notional rent of own premises charged in cost accounts | 36,000 |  |
| Loss on sale of old machinery (not in cost accounts) |  | 20,000 |
| Closing stock: cost accounts ₹1,40,000, financial accounts ₹1,30,000 |  | 10,000 |
| Opening stock: cost accounts ₹90,000, financial accounts ₹1,00,000 |  | 10,000 |
| **Total** | 5,03,000 | 73,000 |

Profit as per financial accounts = 5,03,000 - 73,000 = ₹4,30,000.

questions.prompt: How is the notional rent of ₹36,000 treated in the reconciliation that starts with costing profit?
options: Added, because it reduced only the costing profit
Deducted, because it is an expense
Deducted, because financial profit is lower
questions.explanation: Notional rent is charged only in cost accounts. Costing profit is lower by ₹36,000, so financial profit is higher; add it back.

questions.prompt: How is the closing stock difference treated?
questions.explanation: Closing stock is lower in financial accounts (₹1,30,000 vs ₹1,40,000). Lower closing stock means lower profit in financial books, so deduct ₹10,000.

questions.prompt: How is the opening stock difference treated?
options: Deduct ₹10,000, because higher opening stock in financial accounts reduces financial profit
Add ₹10,000, because opening stock is higher in financial accounts
Add ₹10,000, because closing and opening differences always offset
Ignore it, because it relates to last year
questions.explanation: Opening stock is a debit in the trading account. ₹1,00,000 in financial books against ₹90,000 in cost books means financial profit is ₹10,000 lower: deduct.

questions.prompt: What is the total of items to be ADDED to costing profit in the reconciliation? Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation: Over-absorbed administration overheads 12,000 + interest received 35,000 + notional rent 36,000 = ₹83,000.

questions.prompt: In a non-integrated system, the entry for materials purchased on credit is:
options: Stores Ledger Control A/c Dr, To Cost Ledger Control A/c
Stores Ledger Control A/c Dr, To Creditors A/c
Cost Ledger Control A/c Dr, To Stores Ledger Control A/c
WIP Control A/c Dr, To Cost Ledger Control A/c
questions.explanation: The cost ledger has no personal accounts. The Cost Ledger Control account stands in for creditors. Under an integrated system the credit would be to Creditors.

questions.prompt: Which item appears only in the financial accounts?
questions.explanation: Dividend received is a financial income unrelated to production. Notional interest appears only in cost accounts; the other two are in both.

questions.prompt: From the transactions below (non-integrated system), compute the amount of factory overheads under-absorbed. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.data:
| Transaction | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Materials purchased on credit | 5,00,000 |
| Direct materials issued | 3,80,000 |
| Indirect materials issued | 40,000 |
| Wages paid (direct ₹2,00,000; indirect ₹50,000) | 2,50,000 |
| Factory overheads incurred | 1,60,000 |
| Factory overheads absorbed | 2,40,000 |
| Cost of finished goods completed | 7,00,000 |
| Cost of goods sold | 6,50,000 |
| Sales | 8,00,000 |

questions.prompt: Using the same transactions (no opening balances), compute the closing balance of the WIP Control Account. Round to the nearest rupee.

questions.prompt: Under an integrated accounting system, there is no need to reconcile cost and financial profits.
questions.explanation: There is only one set of books, so only one profit figure exists.

questions.prompt: Which items are excluded from cost accounts?
questions.explanation: Appropriations, capital losses, donations and financial incomes do not relate to the cost of production. Indirect wages are part of overheads.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: in a non-integrated system, the account in the cost ledger that represents all accounts kept in the financial ledger is the Cost Ledger ___ Account.
questions.explanation: It is also called the General Ledger Adjustment Account. It keeps the cost ledger self-balancing.

Closing balances: Stores ₹80,000, WIP ₹1,20,000, Finished goods ₹50,000.

questions.prompt: What is integrated accounting? State its advantages and the prerequisites for installing it.
questions.answer:
- Integrated accounting keeps cost and financial records in **one set of books**, so the same accounts provide cost data and financial statements.
- **Advantages**: no duplication of records; no reconciliation of profits; quicker reports; lower clerical cost; consistent figures; better use of mechanised or computerised accounting.
- **Prerequisites**: decide the extent of integration (up to prime cost or complete integration); a common coding system for accounts and cost centres; agreed procedures for documents such as material requisitions and job cards; perpetual inventory records; staff co-ordination between cost and financial accounting.
- Control accounts for stores, WIP, finished goods and overheads are maintained in the main ledger.

questions.prompt: Why do profits shown by cost accounts and financial accounts differ in a non-integrated system?
questions.answer:
- **Items only in financial accounts**: incomes like interest, dividends, rent received, profit on sale of assets; expenses like fines, losses on sale of assets, goodwill or preliminary expenses written off, donations, income tax and other appropriations.
- **Items only in cost accounts**: notional charges such as rent of owned premises and interest on owners' capital.
- **Under or over absorption** of overheads, because cost accounts use predetermined rates while financial accounts record actual expenses.
- **Different stock valuation**: cost accounts may use FIFO or weighted average and include production overheads differently; financial accounts use lower of cost and net realisable value.
- **Different depreciation** methods or rates.
- The differences are shown in a reconciliation statement or memorandum reconciliation account.

chapters.title: Job, Batch and Contract Costing
chapters.summary: Specific order costing: job cost sheets and quotations, batch costing with economic batch quantity, and contract accounts with profit on incomplete contracts.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Job costing
lesson.body:
**Job costing** is used where work is done to customer specification, each job is distinct and identifiable, and work moves through departments as a separate order: printing, repair shops, furniture to order, interior decoration, machine tools to order.

Procedure: receive enquiry and quote a price; on getting the order, issue a **production order** with a job number; collect material (from material requisitions), labour (from job cards) and overheads (at predetermined rates) on a **job cost sheet**; on completion, compare cost with price.

Quotation workings follow the cost sheet: material + labour + works overheads = works cost; + administration overheads = cost of production; + profit = price. Rates for overheads come from past data or budgets.

**Spoiled and defective work in jobs**: normal spoilage is absorbed by the job (or overheads); spoilage due to customer change of specification is charged to that job; abnormal spoilage goes to costing P&L.

lesson.heading: Batch costing and EBQ
lesson.body:
**Batch costing** treats a batch of identical units as the cost unit: pharmaceuticals, biscuits, garments, components. Cost per unit = batch cost / units in the batch.

Each batch needs a set-up. Larger batches mean fewer set-ups but more stock to carry. The **Economic Batch Quantity**:

`EBQ = sqrt(2DS / C)`, where D = annual demand, S = set-up cost per batch, C = carrying cost per unit per year.

Example: D = 24,000 units, S = ₹1,500, C = ₹2. EBQ = sqrt(2 x 24,000 x 1,500 / 2) = sqrt(3,60,00,000) = 6,000 units, so 4 batches a year.

lesson.heading: Contract costing
lesson.body:
**Contract costing** is job costing for large, long, mostly site-based work: buildings, roads, bridges, ships. Each contract has its own account. Features: most costs are direct (even site supervision, telephone, power); plant at site is charged either by hire or by depreciation; payment is made in stages against **work certified** by the architect, less **retention money** held as security.

Key terms:

- **Work certified**: value (at contract price) of work approved by the architect.
- **Work uncertified**: work done but not yet certified, shown at **cost**.
- **Notional profit** = work certified + cost of work uncertified - cost of work to date.
- **Escalation clause**: protects the contractor against specified rises in prices of inputs.
- **Cost-plus contract**: price = actual cost + agreed % profit; common for government work or where cost cannot be estimated.

Profit credited to P&L on an incomplete contract (traditional costing approach):

| Stage of completion (work certified / contract price) | Profit taken to P&L |
| --- | --- |
| Less than 25% | Nil; whole notional profit to reserve |
| 25% to less than 50% | 1/3 x notional profit x cash received / work certified |
| 50% to less than 90% | 2/3 x notional profit x cash received / work certified |
| 90% or more (nearly complete) | Estimated total profit x work certified / contract price (or a similar formula) |

A **loss** on a contract is charged to P&L in full at once.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Contract price ₹1,20,00,000. Cost to date ₹60,00,000 (net of material at site). Work certified ₹66,00,000, uncertified at cost ₹3,00,000, cash received 90% of certified.

- Completion = 66 / 120 = 55%, so the 2/3 rule applies.
- Notional profit = 66,00,000 + 3,00,000 - 60,00,000 = ₹9,00,000.
- Profit to P&L = 2/3 x 9,00,000 x 59,40,000 / 66,00,000 = ₹5,40,000; reserve ₹3,60,000.

Common mistakes:

- Valuing uncertified work at contract price instead of cost.
- Forgetting to deduct material and plant lying at site at year end from cost.
- Using cash received / contract price instead of cash received / work certified.
- Charging abnormal losses (fire, theft) to the contract instead of costing P&L.

keyPoints: Notional profit = work certified + work uncertified (at cost) - cost to date.
Profit to P&L: below 25% nil; 25-50% one-third; 50-90% two-thirds, each x cash received / work certified.
Any expected loss on a contract is taken to P&L in full.
Retention money = work certified - cash received.
EBQ = sqrt(2DS/C).
Job costing: each job is a cost unit; batch costing: the batch is the cost unit.

cases.title: Case: Shivam Builders, Contract 12
cases.body:
Shivam Builders started Contract 12 (contract price ₹1,20,00,000) during the year. Data at year end:

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Materials sent to site | 32,00,000 |
| Wages | 22,00,000 |
| Hire charges of plant | 4,00,000 |
| Site overheads | 4,00,000 |
| Materials at site at year end | 2,00,000 |
| Work certified | 66,00,000 |
| Work done but not certified, at cost | 3,00,000 |

The contractee has paid 90% of the work certified. Profit on incomplete contracts is recognised using the stage-of-completion fractions.

questions.prompt: Compute the notional profit on Contract 12. Round to the nearest rupee.
What is the stage of completion and which fraction applies?
options: 55%: two-thirds of notional profit adjusted for cash received
55%: one-third of notional profit adjusted for cash received
questions.explanation: Completion = work certified / contract price = 66,00,000 / 1,20,00,000 = 55%. Between 50% and 90%, take 2/3 x notional profit x cash received / work certified. Uncertified work is not included in the stage of completion.

questions.prompt: Compute the profit to be credited to the profit and loss account for the year. Round to the nearest rupee.
What is the retention money held by the contractee?
questions.explanation: Retention = work certified - cash received = 66,00,000 - 59,40,000 = ₹6,60,000 (10% of work certified).

questions.prompt: Suppose materials costing ₹50,000 at the Contract 12 site were destroyed by fire. How is this treated?
options: Credited to the contract account and debited to costing P&L
Left in the contract account as part of cost
questions.explanation: Destruction by fire is abnormal. It is removed from the contract (credit) and written off to costing P&L so that contract profit is not distorted.

questions.prompt: Compute the economic batch quantity.
questions.data: Annual demand 24,000 units. Set-up cost ₹1,500 per batch. Carrying cost ₹2 per unit per year.

questions.prompt: A job needs direct material ₹40,000 and 200 labour hours at ₹120. Works overheads are ₹80 per labour hour and administration overheads 10% of works cost. What price gives a profit of 20% on the selling price?
questions.explanation: Labour 24,000; works overheads 16,000; works cost ₹80,000; administration 8,000; total cost ₹88,000. Price = 88,000 / 0.80 = ₹1,10,000. (₹1,05,600 wrongly adds 20% on cost.)

questions.prompt: Batch costing is most suitable for:
options: A pharmaceutical company making tablets in lots
A repair workshop doing customer jobs
questions.explanation: Tablets are made in batches of identical units, so the batch is the cost unit. Shipbuilding is contract costing, repairs are job costing and refining is process costing.

questions.prompt: In a cost-plus contract, the contractor bears the risk of increase in the cost of inputs.
questions.explanation: In a cost-plus contract the contractee pays actual cost plus an agreed margin, so cost increases are passed on. The risk lies with the contractee.

questions.prompt: Which are features of contract costing?
options: Work is mostly done at the customer's site
Progress payments are made against work certified
Each unit of output is identical
questions.explanation: Identical units belong to process or batch costing. Contracts are unique, site-based and paid in stages with retention.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a clause in a contract that allows the price to be raised if specified input prices rise is called an ___ clause.
questions.explanation: An escalation clause protects the contractor; a de-escalation clause may also allow a reduction if prices fall.

questions.prompt: Prepare the contract account for the year and show the profit to be credited to P&L.
questions.data: Contract price ₹50,00,000. Materials sent to site ₹10,00,000; wages ₹8,00,000; site overheads ₹2,50,000; plant sent to site at the start of the year ₹3,00,000 (depreciation 20% a year). Materials at site at year end ₹50,000. Work certified ₹20,00,000; work uncertified at cost ₹1,00,000. Cash received ₹15,00,000.
questions.answer:
| Dr | ₹ | Cr | ₹ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| To Materials | 10,00,000 | By Materials at site c/d | 50,000 |
| To Wages | 8,00,000 | By Plant at site c/d (3,00,000 - 60,000) | 2,40,000 |
| To Site overheads | 2,50,000 | By Work-in-progress: certified | 20,00,000 |
| To Plant | 3,00,000 | By Work-in-progress: uncertified | 1,00,000 |
| To Notional profit c/d | 40,000 |  |  |
| **Total** | 23,90,000 | **Total** | 23,90,000 |
| To Costing P&L | 10,000 | By Notional profit b/d | 40,000 |
| To Work-in-progress (reserve) | 30,000 |  |  |

Workings: completion = 20,00,000 / 50,00,000 = 40%, so one-third rule. Profit to P&L = 1/3 x 40,000 x 15,00,000 / 20,00,000 = ₹10,000. Reserve ₹30,000.

Balance sheet: WIP = certified 20,00,000 + uncertified 1,00,000 - reserve 30,000 - cash received 15,00,000 = ₹5,70,000.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between job costing and contract costing.
questions.answer:
- **Nature of work**: job costing for small, short jobs usually done in the factory; contract costing for large, long-duration work done mostly at site.
- **Duration**: jobs usually finish within the accounting period; contracts often run over more than one year, so profit on incomplete contracts must be estimated.
- **Costs**: in job costing many costs are indirect and absorbed via overheads; in contracts most costs (site staff, power, plant) are direct.
- **Payment**: jobs are billed on completion; contracts get progress payments against work certified, less retention money.
- **Number of units**: a job shop runs many jobs at once; a contractor handles a few large contracts.
- **Profit**: job profit is known at completion; contract profit is recognised in stages.

questions.prompt: Explain cost-plus contracts with their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.answer:
- A cost-plus contract fixes price as actual cost plus an agreed percentage or fixed fee as profit. Used where cost cannot be estimated reliably: defence, new technology, government work, emergency repairs.
- **Advantages to the contractor**: no risk of loss from cost increases; assured profit.
- **Advantages to the contractee**: pays a fair price based on actual cost; can inspect cost records.
- **Disadvantages**: the contractor has no incentive to control cost (higher cost raises his profit when it is a percentage); the contractee cannot know the final price in advance; detailed cost records and audit are needed.
- A fixed fee instead of a percentage reduces the incentive to inflate cost.
