chapters.title: Process and Operation Costing, Joint and By-Products
chapters.summary: Process accounts with normal and abnormal loss or gain, equivalent production under FIFO and weighted average, operation costing, and costing of joint products and by-products.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Process costing and process losses
lesson.body:
**Process costing** is used where identical units pass through a sequence of processes: chemicals, textiles, sugar, cement, oil refining, paper. The output of one process is the input (raw material) of the next. A **process account** is kept for each process.

Losses:

- **Normal loss**: expected and unavoidable (evaporation, shrinkage). Its cost is borne by good units. Only its scrap value is credited to the process account.
- **Abnormal loss**: actual loss above normal (accidents, bad material). Valued like good units and transferred to an Abnormal Loss account; its scrap value is credited there and the balance goes to costing P&L.
- **Abnormal gain**: actual loss below normal. Valued like good units and debited to the process; the Abnormal Gain account is credited with it, debited with the scrap value lost on normal loss not realised, and the net credited to costing P&L.

`Cost per unit = (total process cost - scrap value of normal loss) / (input units - normal loss units)`

Abnormal loss and abnormal gain units are valued at this same cost per unit.

lesson.heading: Equivalent production
lesson.body:
When work is incomplete at period end, units are converted into **equivalent units** (EU) = units x % completion, separately for material and conversion cost (labour + overheads).

| Method | Opening WIP | Cost per EU |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FIFO | Completed first. Only the work needed to finish it this period counts (units x % remaining). | Current period cost / current EU |
| Weighted average | Merged with current units; all completed units count as 100%. | (Opening WIP cost + current cost) / total EU |

FIFO statement of equivalent production splits output into: (a) opening WIP completed, (b) units started and completed (completed - opening WIP), (c) closing WIP, (d) abnormal loss if any (usually 100% complete). Normal loss gets no equivalent units.

Example: opening WIP 2,000 units (material 100%, conversion 60%), introduced 18,000, completed 17,000, closing WIP 3,000 (material 100%, conversion 40%). FIFO conversion EU = 2,000 x 40% + 15,000 + 3,000 x 40% = 17,000. Weighted average conversion EU = 17,000 + 1,200 = 18,200.

lesson.heading: Operation costing, joint products and by-products
lesson.body:
**Operation costing** is a refinement of process costing that finds the cost of each operation (cutting, drilling, polishing) within a process, useful for mass production of standard components.

**Joint products** are two or more products of significant value produced together from the same input up to a **split-off point** (petrol, diesel and kerosene; milk and cream). Joint costs up to split-off are apportioned by:

- Physical units (output quantity)
- Sales value at split-off
- **Net realisable value** = final sales value - further processing and selling costs after split-off
- Constant gross profit margin (same overall GP % for every product)

**By-products** are of small value compared with main products (molasses in sugar, sawdust in timber). Treatment: NRV of by-product credited to the main process (most common); sales treated as other income; or the reverse cost method (sales value less profit margin and post-split costs credited to the joint process).

**Further processing decision**: process further only if incremental revenue exceeds incremental cost. Joint costs are irrelevant to this decision.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Input 10,000 kg at ₹40, labour ₹1,20,000, overheads ₹80,000. Normal loss 10%, scrap ₹15 per kg. Output 8,800 kg.

| Process A Account | Kg | ₹ |  | Kg | ₹ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| To Material | 10,000 | 4,00,000 | By Normal loss (scrap) | 1,000 | 15,000 |
| To Labour |  | 1,20,000 | By Abnormal loss (at ₹65) | 200 | 13,000 |
| To Overheads |  | 80,000 | By Process B (at ₹65) | 8,800 | 5,72,000 |
| **Total** | 10,000 | 6,00,000 | **Total** | 10,000 | 6,00,000 |

Cost per kg = (6,00,000 - 15,000) / 9,000 = ₹65. Net abnormal loss to costing P&L = 13,000 - 200 x 15 = ₹10,000.

Common mistakes:

- Valuing abnormal loss at scrap value instead of at the cost of good units.
- Giving equivalent units to normal loss.
- Under FIFO, counting opening WIP as 100% complete.
- Using joint costs in further-processing decisions.

keyPoints: Cost per unit = (total cost - scrap value of normal loss) / (input - normal loss).
Abnormal loss and gain are valued at the same cost per unit as good output.
Net abnormal loss (after scrap) and net abnormal gain go to costing P&L.
FIFO EU for opening WIP = units x % work remaining; weighted average treats all completed units as 100%.
Normal loss gets no equivalent units; abnormal loss does.
NRV = final sales value - post split-off costs; joint costs are irrelevant to further processing decisions.

cases.title: Case: Sagar Chemicals, Process A
cases.body: Sagar Chemicals put 10,000 kg of raw material at ₹40 per kg into Process A. Labour cost was ₹1,20,000 and overheads ₹80,000. Normal loss is 10% of input, and scrap sells at ₹15 per kg. Actual output transferred to Process B was 8,800 kg. There was no opening or closing work-in-progress.

questions.prompt: Compute the cost per kg of normal output, to 2 decimals.
How many kg of abnormal loss or gain arose, and what is the value of output transferred to Process B?
questions.explanation: Expected output = 10,000 - 1,000 = 9,000 kg. Actual 8,800, so abnormal loss = 200 kg. Transfer = 8,800 x 65 = ₹5,72,000.

questions.prompt: Compute the net amount of abnormal loss charged to the costing profit and loss account. Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation: Abnormal loss valued at 200 x 65 = ₹13,000. Less scrap realised 200 x 15 = ₹3,000. Net to costing P&L = ₹10,000.

questions.prompt: If actual output had been 9,200 kg instead, what would the result be?
options: Abnormal gain of 200 kg valued at ₹13,000; net ₹10,000 credited to costing P&L
Abnormal gain of 200 kg valued at ₹3,000
Abnormal gain of 200 kg; net ₹13,000 credited to costing P&L
No abnormal gain because normal loss is only an estimate
questions.explanation: Gain = 9,200 - 9,000 = 200 kg, valued at ₹65 = ₹13,000 and debited to Process A. The Abnormal Gain account is charged with the scrap not realised (200 x 15 = ₹3,000), so net ₹10,000 goes to costing P&L.

questions.prompt: The scrap value of the 1,000 kg normal loss is credited to the Process A account.
questions.explanation: Normal loss carries no cost; only its realisable value of ₹15,000 is credited to the process, which lowers the cost of good units.

questions.prompt: Under FIFO, compute the equivalent units for conversion cost.
questions.data: Opening WIP 2,000 units (material 100%, conversion 60%). Units introduced 18,000. Units completed and transferred 17,000. Closing WIP 3,000 units (material 100%, conversion 40%). No process losses.
questions.explanation:
| Output | Units | Conversion % | EU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Opening WIP completed | 2,000 | 40% | 800 |
| Started and completed (17,000 - 2,000) | 15,000 | 100% | 15,000 |
| Closing WIP | 3,000 | 40% | 1,200 |
| **Total** | 20,000 |  | 17,000 |

questions.prompt: With the same data (opening WIP 2,000 units at 60% conversion, completed 17,000, closing WIP 3,000 at 40% conversion), what are the conversion equivalent units under the weighted average method?
questions.explanation: Weighted average treats all 17,000 completed units as 100% done: 17,000 + 3,000 x 40% = 18,200.

questions.prompt: Apportion the joint cost using the net realisable value method. How much joint cost is charged to product X? Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.data:
| Product | Units | Final price (₹) | Further processing cost after split-off (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| X | 5,000 | 150 | 1,50,000 |
| Y | 10,000 | 60 | 2,00,000 |

Joint cost up to split-off: ₹6,00,000.

questions.prompt: Under the most common method of accounting for a by-product of small value, its net realisable value is:
options: Credited to the main process account, reducing the cost of the main product
Added to the cost of the main product
Treated as a joint product and given a share of joint cost
questions.explanation: The by-product's NRV is a recovery that reduces the cost of the main product. Alternatively, small sales may be shown as other income.

questions.prompt: Which are accepted methods of apportioning joint costs?
questions.explanation: The machine hour rate is an overhead absorption method. The other four apportion joint costs.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the point in a joint process after which the products can be identified separately is called the ___ point.
questions.explanation: Costs before the split-off point are joint costs; costs after it are separable costs of each product.

questions.prompt: Using FIFO, prepare the statement of equivalent production, statement of cost per equivalent unit, and statement of evaluation for Process B.
questions.data: Opening WIP 2,000 units (material 100%, conversion 60%), value ₹50,000. Units introduced 18,000; material cost ₹3,60,000; conversion cost ₹3,40,000. Completed and transferred 17,000 units. Closing WIP 3,000 units (material 100%, conversion 40%). No losses.
questions.answer:
**Statement of equivalent production (FIFO)**

| Output | Units | Material % | Material EU | Conversion % | Conversion EU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Opening WIP completed | 2,000 | - | - | 40% | 800 |
| Started and completed | 15,000 | 100% | 15,000 | 100% | 15,000 |
| Closing WIP | 3,000 | 100% | 3,000 | 40% | 1,200 |
| **Total** | 20,000 |  | 18,000 |  | 17,000 |

**Cost per EU**: material 3,60,000 / 18,000 = ₹20; conversion 3,40,000 / 17,000 = ₹20.

**Statement of evaluation**

| Item | Working | ₹ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opening WIP completed | 50,000 + 800 x 20 | 66,000 |
| Started and completed | 15,000 x 40 | 6,00,000 |
| **Transferred to next process (17,000 units)** |  | 6,66,000 |
| Closing WIP | 3,000 x 20 + 1,200 x 20 | 84,000 |
| **Total (check: 50,000 + 3,60,000 + 3,40,000)** |  | 7,50,000 |

questions.prompt: Distinguish between joint products and by-products, and explain the methods of accounting for by-products.
questions.answer:
- **Joint products** are two or more products of significant and comparable value produced together from the same process; none is clearly the main product (petrol and diesel).
- **By-products** are incidental products of small value relative to the main product (molasses from sugar, sawdust from timber).
- Joint costs are apportioned among joint products (physical units, sales value at split-off, NRV, constant gross margin); by-products usually receive no share of joint costs.
- **By-product methods**: (a) sales value or NRV credited to the main process (other income method for negligible values); (b) NRV method: sales less post-separation costs credited to the joint process; (c) reverse cost method: sales value less estimated profit and post-split costs credited to the joint process; (d) where significant, treated like a joint product with a share of joint cost.
- Classification depends on relative value and management's intent, and can change over time.

questions.prompt: Explain the treatment of normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain in process accounts.
questions.answer:
- **Normal loss** is the unavoidable loss expected under normal conditions. Its quantity is credited to the process at scrap value only; its cost is absorbed by good output.
- **Abnormal loss** is loss beyond normal. It is valued at the cost per unit of good output, credited to the process and debited to the Abnormal Loss account; scrap realised is credited to that account and the balance written off to costing P&L.
- **Abnormal gain** arises when actual loss is less than normal. It is valued at the cost of good output and debited to the process; the Abnormal Gain account is debited with the scrap value of normal loss not realised; the net is credited to costing P&L.
- Cost per unit = (total cost - scrap value of normal loss) / (input - normal loss units).
- This keeps the cost of good units at its normal level and shows abnormal items separately for control.

chapters.title: Service Costing and Standard Costing
chapters.summary: Cost units and cost sheets for transport, hotels and hospitals, and standard costing with material, labour and overhead variance analysis.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Service costing
lesson.body:
**Service (operating) costing** finds the cost of providing a service: transport, power, hotels, hospitals, canteens, IT services, toll roads. Services cannot be stored, costs are mostly fixed, and the cost unit is often **composite** (two measures multiplied).

| Service | Cost unit |
| --- | --- |
| Goods transport | Tonne-km |
| Passenger transport | Passenger-km |
| Hotel | Room-day (or room-night) |
| Hospital | Patient-day, bed-day |
| Power | kWh |
| Canteen | Meal served |

Transport cost sheet groups costs as: **standing (fixed) charges** (driver and conductor salaries if fixed, insurance, road tax, garage rent, depreciation on time basis, interest), **maintenance charges** (repairs, tyres, overhaul) and **running charges** (fuel, oil, depreciation on km basis).

Tonne-km:

- **Absolute tonne-km** = sum of (distance of each leg x weight carried on that leg).
- **Commercial tonne-km** = total distance x average load (average of the loads on each leg, including empty legs).

Passenger-km = distance x seating capacity x % occupancy x number of trips.

lesson.heading: Standard costing basics
lesson.body:
A **standard cost** is a predetermined cost of what a unit should cost under efficient conditions. Comparing actual with standard gives **variances**, which are investigated by **management by exception** (only significant variances get attention).

Types of standards: ideal (perfect conditions, rarely met), basic (fixed long-term base), current or expected (attainable with reasonable effort; most used).

Notation: SQ = standard quantity for actual output, SP = standard price, AQ = actual quantity, AP = actual price; SH = standard hours for actual output, SR = standard rate, AH = actual hours. Variance is favourable (F) when actual cost is below standard and adverse (A) when above.

lesson.heading: Variance formulas
lesson.body:
| Variance | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Material cost | SQ x SP - AQ x AP |
| Material price | AQ x (SP - AP) |
| Material usage | SP x (SQ - AQ) |
| Material mix (part of usage) | SP x (revised SQ - AQ), revised SQ = total AQ in standard ratio |
| Material yield (part of usage) | SP x (SQ - revised SQ) |
| Labour cost | SH x SR - AH paid x AR |
| Labour rate | AH paid x (SR - AR) |
| Labour idle time | Idle hours x SR (always adverse) |
| Labour efficiency | SR x (SH - AH worked) |
| Variable overhead cost | Absorbed (SH x SR) - actual |
| Variable overhead expenditure | AH worked x SR - actual |
| Variable overhead efficiency | SR x (SH - AH worked) |
| Fixed overhead cost | Absorbed (actual output x standard rate per unit) - actual |
| Fixed overhead expenditure | Budgeted - actual |
| Fixed overhead volume | Absorbed - budgeted (split into efficiency and capacity) |

Always check that the sub-variances add up to the total variance.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Standard: 4 kg at ₹50 and 3 hours at ₹80 per unit. Output 2,000 units. Actual: 8,300 kg at ₹48; 6,200 hours paid at ₹85, of which 300 hours idle.

- SQ = 8,000 kg; material price variance = 8,300 x (50 - 48) = ₹16,600 F; usage = 50 x (8,000 - 8,300) = ₹15,000 A; cost = ₹1,600 F.
- SH = 6,000; rate = 6,200 x (80 - 85) = ₹31,000 A; idle time = 300 x 80 = ₹24,000 A; efficiency = 80 x (6,000 - 5,900) = ₹8,000 F; cost = ₹47,000 A.

Common mistakes:

- Using standard quantity for budgeted output instead of actual output.
- Computing labour efficiency on hours paid rather than hours worked when there is idle time.
- Computing commercial tonne-km on loaded legs only and ignoring the empty return leg in the average.
- Mixing up signs: state F or A for every variance.

keyPoints: Material price = AQ(SP - AP); usage = SP(SQ - AQ); SQ is for actual output.
Labour rate = AH paid(SR - AR); efficiency = SR(SH - AH worked); idle time = idle hours x SR, always adverse.
Fixed overhead volume = absorbed - budgeted; expenditure = budgeted - actual.
Absolute tonne-km = sum of km x load per leg; commercial = total km x average load.
Passenger-km = km x seats x occupancy %.
Sub-variances must reconcile to the total variance.

cases.title: Case: Unnati Industries, product Z
cases.body:
Standard cost card of product Z (per unit):

| Element | Standard |
| --- | --- |
| Direct material | 4 kg at ₹50 per kg |
| Direct labour | 3 hours at ₹80 per hour |

Actual results for March: output 2,000 units. Material used 8,300 kg bought at ₹48 per kg. Labour paid for 6,200 hours at ₹85 per hour, which includes 300 hours of abnormal idle time due to a machine breakdown.

questions.prompt: Compute the material price variance (enter the amount only; it is favourable).
Compute the material usage variance (enter the amount only; it is adverse).
Compute the labour efficiency variance (enter the amount only; it is favourable).
What is the labour cost variance?
questions.explanation: Standard cost = 6,000 x 80 = 4,80,000. Actual = 6,200 x 85 = 5,27,000. LCV = ₹47,000 A = rate 31,000 A + idle time 24,000 A + efficiency 8,000 F.

questions.prompt: What is the labour idle time variance?
questions.explanation: Idle time variance = idle hours x standard rate = 300 x 80 = ₹24,000, always adverse. Using the actual rate (₹25,500) is wrong because the rate difference is already in the rate variance.

questions.prompt: Compute the absolute tonne-km for the trip.
questions.data:
| Leg | Distance (km) | Load (tonnes) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A to B | 120 | 8 |
| B to C | 80 | 5 |
| C to A | 200 | Empty |

questions.prompt: For the same trip (A to B 120 km with 8 tonnes, B to C 80 km with 5 tonnes, C to A 200 km empty), what are the commercial tonne-km?
questions.explanation: Commercial tonne-km = total distance x average load = 400 x (8 + 5 + 0) / 3 = 1733.33.

questions.prompt: Budgeted fixed overheads are ₹2,40,000 for 12,000 units. Actual output was 11,000 units and actual fixed overheads ₹2,50,000. What is the fixed overhead volume variance?
questions.explanation: Standard rate ₹20 per unit. Absorbed = 11,000 x 20 = ₹2,20,000. Volume = absorbed - budgeted = 2,20,000 - 2,40,000 = ₹20,000 A. Expenditure = 2,40,000 - 2,50,000 = ₹10,000 A. Total ₹30,000 A.

questions.prompt: Labour idle time variance is always adverse.
questions.explanation: Idle hours are paid for but produce nothing, so they can only add cost.

questions.prompt: Which are composite cost units?
questions.explanation: A composite unit combines two measures (passengers and km, tonnes and km, patients and days). kWh and per meal are simple units.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the practice of focusing management attention only on significant deviations from standard is called management by ___.
questions.explanation: Variance reports highlight significant variances so managers investigate only those.

questions.prompt: Compute the cost per passenger-km of operating a city bus, to 2 decimals.
questions.data: Cost of bus ₹25,00,000, life 5 years, scrap value ₹5,00,000 (straight line). Driver's salary ₹30,000 a month; conductor's salary ₹20,000 a month. Insurance ₹60,000 a year; road tax ₹40,000 a year; garage rent ₹6,000 a month; repairs and maintenance ₹1,20,000 a year. The bus runs 200 km a day for 25 days a month, giving 4 km per litre of diesel costing ₹90 a litre. It has 50 seats and runs on average 80% full.
questions.answer:
| Operating cost statement (annual) | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| **A. Standing charges** |  |
| Depreciation (25,00,000 - 5,00,000) / 5 | 4,00,000 |
| Driver (30,000 x 12) | 3,60,000 |
| Conductor (20,000 x 12) | 2,40,000 |
| Insurance | 60,000 |
| Road tax | 40,000 |
| Garage rent (6,000 x 12) | 72,000 |
| Total standing charges | 11,72,000 |
| **B. Maintenance charges**: repairs | 1,20,000 |
| **C. Running charges**: diesel (60,000 km / 4 x ₹90) | 13,50,000 |
| **Total operating cost** | 26,42,000 |

Annual km = 200 x 25 x 12 = 60,000. Passenger-km = 60,000 x 50 x 80% = 24,00,000.

Cost per passenger-km = 26,42,000 / 24,00,000 = **₹1.1008, about ₹1.10**.

questions.prompt: What is standard costing? Explain its advantages and limitations.
questions.answer:
- Standard costing sets predetermined costs for material, labour and overheads per unit, records actual costs, and analyses the variances by cause and responsibility.
- **Advantages**: control through management by exception; fixes responsibility (price variances to purchasing, usage and efficiency to production); a basis for pricing and budgeting; simpler stock valuation; encourages cost consciousness and efficiency.
- **Limitations**: setting accurate standards is difficult and costly; standards go out of date when prices or methods change; unsuitable where products are non-standard; ideal standards can demotivate staff; variances may be caused by factors outside a manager's control.
- Attainable (current) standards are most commonly used.

questions.prompt: State the main features of service costing and how costs are classified in a transport cost sheet.
questions.answer:
- Services cannot be stored, so cost is measured per unit of service delivered.
- A large share of cost is fixed and capital cost is often high.
- Cost units are often composite: passenger-km, tonne-km, patient-day, room-day.
- Costs are classified to show which are fixed and which vary with use.
- **Transport cost sheet**: standing charges (salaries, insurance, road tax, garage rent, time-based depreciation, interest); maintenance charges (repairs, tyres, overhauls); running charges (fuel, oil, km-based depreciation, running wages).
- The cost per unit helps fix fares and freight rates, compare vehicles and routes, and control cost.

chapters.title: Marginal Costing, Budgets and Budgetary Control
chapters.summary: Marginal versus absorption costing, CVP analysis and break-even, short-term decisions with a key factor, and functional, flexible and zero-based budgets.
chapters.applicableFor: ICAI new scheme, May 2027 attempt onward

lesson.heading: Marginal costing and absorption costing
lesson.body:
**Marginal costing** charges only variable costs to products; fixed costs are period costs written off in full against contribution. **Contribution** = sales - variable cost = fixed cost + profit.

Under **absorption costing**, fixed production overheads are included in product cost, so part of them is carried forward in closing stock.

- Production > sales (stock rises): absorption profit is higher.
- Production < sales (stock falls): marginal profit is higher.
- Production = sales: profits are equal.

Difference in profit = change in stock units x fixed production overhead per unit.

Example: production 10,000, sales 8,000, fixed production overheads ₹3,00,000 (₹30 a unit at normal capacity of 10,000). Absorption profit is higher by 2,000 x 30 = ₹60,000.

lesson.heading: CVP analysis
lesson.body:
| Measure | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| P/V ratio | Contribution / sales x 100 = change in profit / change in sales x 100 |
| Break-even point (units) | Fixed cost / contribution per unit |
| Break-even sales (₹) | Fixed cost / P/V ratio |
| Margin of safety | Actual sales - break-even sales = profit / P/V ratio |
| Sales for target profit | (Fixed cost + target profit) / contribution per unit (or / P/V ratio for ₹) |
| Profit | Sales x P/V ratio - fixed cost = margin of safety x P/V ratio |

Worked example: price ₹500, variable cost ₹300, fixed cost ₹24,00,000. Contribution ₹200, P/V 40%. BEP = 24,00,000 / 200 = 12,000 units = ₹60,00,000. At 15,000 units, margin of safety = ₹15,00,000 (20%) and profit = 15,00,000 x 40% = ₹6,00,000.

Assumptions: costs split cleanly into fixed and variable, selling price constant, constant sales mix, no change in stock. A price cut lowers contribution per unit and raises the BEP.

lesson.heading: Decision making
lesson.body:
Relevant costs are future costs that differ between alternatives. Fixed costs that do not change are irrelevant.

- **Key (limiting) factor**: when a resource such as machine hours, labour or material is scarce, rank products by **contribution per unit of the key factor**, not by contribution per unit.
- **Make or buy**: buy if the purchase price is below the variable (marginal) cost of making plus any avoidable fixed cost, and consider the opportunity cost of freed capacity.
- **Accept a special order** below normal price if it covers marginal cost and spare capacity exists, without affecting regular sales.
- **Shut down or continue**: continue in the short run while contribution covers avoidable fixed costs (shut-down point = avoidable fixed cost / contribution per unit).
- **Product mix and dropping a product**: drop only if its contribution is negative or the freed resources earn more elsewhere.

lesson.heading: Budgets and budgetary control
lesson.body:
A **budget** is a quantitative plan for a future period. **Budgetary control** compares actual with budget and acts on differences.

- **Principal budget factor (key factor)**: the factor limiting activity, usually sales; it is budgeted first.
- **Functional budgets**: sales, production, material purchase, labour, overheads, cash. They combine into the **master budget** (budgeted P&L and balance sheet).
- **Fixed budget**: for one level of activity. **Flexible budget**: recast for the actual level, separating fixed, variable and semi-variable costs; it allows meaningful comparison.
- **Zero-based budgeting (ZBB)**: every activity is justified from zero each period, not on last year's figure plus an increment.
- **Performance budgeting** links spending to measurable outputs.

Budget ratios: efficiency = standard hours for actual output / actual hours x 100; activity = standard hours / budgeted hours x 100; capacity = actual hours / budgeted hours x 100. Activity ratio = efficiency x capacity.

Common mistakes: keeping a semi-variable cost constant in a flexible budget, ranking products by contribution per unit when a key factor exists, and using total cost (including fixed) for short-term decisions.

keyPoints: Contribution = sales - variable cost = fixed cost + profit.
BEP units = fixed cost / contribution per unit; BEP sales = fixed cost / P/V ratio.
Margin of safety = actual sales - BEP sales = profit / P/V ratio.
Profit difference (absorption vs marginal) = change in stock units x fixed production overhead rate.
With a key factor, rank by contribution per unit of that factor.
Flexible budget: fixed constant, variable per unit, semi-variable split into both parts.
Activity ratio = efficiency ratio x capacity ratio.

cases.title: Case: Pragati Coolers
cases.body: Pragati Coolers sells one model of air cooler at ₹500. Variable cost is ₹300 a unit and annual fixed costs are ₹24,00,000. Last year it sold 15,000 units. Management is reviewing next year's plan.

questions.prompt: Compute the break-even point in units.
What were the P/V ratio and the margin of safety (as a % of sales) last year?
How many units must be sold to earn a profit of ₹9,00,000?
If the price is cut by 10% with no change in costs, what is the new break-even point?
questions.explanation: New price ₹450; contribution ₹150. BEP = 24,00,000 / 150 = 16,000 units.

questions.prompt: Pragati gets a one-time export order for 1,000 units at ₹350 each. It has spare capacity, and regular sales and fixed costs are unaffected. Should it accept?
options: No: price is below total cost per unit of ₹460
questions.explanation: Relevant cost is the variable cost of ₹300. Extra contribution = 1,000 x (350 - 300) = ₹50,000. Fixed cost per unit (₹160 at 15,000 units) is irrelevant because total fixed cost does not change.

questions.prompt: By how much will profit under absorption costing exceed profit under marginal costing? Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.data: Opening stock nil. Production 10,000 units (normal capacity). Sales 8,000 units. Fixed production overheads ₹3,00,000. Variable costs and price are the same under both methods.
questions.explanation: Fixed production overhead rate = 3,00,000 / 10,000 = ₹30 per unit. Closing stock 2,000 units carries 2,000 x 30 = ₹60,000 of fixed overheads under absorption costing, so its profit is higher by that amount.

questions.prompt: Prepare a flexible budget figure: compute total cost at 80% capacity (8,000 units). Round to the nearest rupee.
questions.data: At 60% capacity (6,000 units): variable cost ₹120 per unit; semi-variable cost ₹1,50,000, of which 40% is fixed; fixed cost ₹2,00,000.

questions.prompt: Budgeted hours 9,000; actual hours worked 10,000; standard hours for actual output 9,500. What is the activity ratio?
Under zero-based budgeting:
options: Every activity must be justified afresh as if it were new, ranked as decision packages
Last year's budget is increased for inflation
Budgets are revised every month for the next twelve months
Budgets show only revenue items, not capital items
questions.explanation: ZBB starts from zero; each decision package is evaluated and ranked by cost and benefit. Monthly rolling forward describes a rolling (continuous) budget.

questions.prompt: Under marginal costing, fixed production overheads are included in the valuation of closing stock.
questions.explanation: Marginal costing values stock at variable cost only. Fixed production overheads are written off in the period incurred.

questions.prompt: Which are relevant in deciding whether to make a component or buy it from outside?
options: Fixed costs that will be avoided if the component is bought
Apportioned general fixed overheads that continue anyway
Contribution from alternative use of the freed capacity
questions.explanation: Unavoidable apportioned fixed overheads do not change with the decision and are irrelevant. Opportunity cost of capacity is relevant.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the factor that limits the activity of a business and is budgeted first (usually sales) is called the principal budget ___.
questions.explanation: It may also be material, labour, machine capacity or finance. All functional budgets depend on it.

questions.prompt: Machine hours are limited to 18,000 a year. Determine the most profitable product mix and the resulting profit.
questions.data:
| Product | Price (₹) | Variable cost (₹) | Machine hours per unit | Maximum demand (units) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 200 | 120 | 4 | 2,000 |
| B | 300 | 180 | 8 | 1,500 |
| C | 150 | 90 | 2 | 3,000 |

Fixed costs ₹2,50,000.
questions.answer:
| Product | Contribution per unit (₹) | Hours per unit | Contribution per hour (₹) | Rank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 80 | 4 | 20 | 2 |
| B | 120 | 8 | 15 | 3 |
| C | 60 | 2 | 30 | 1 |

Allocate hours in rank order:

| Product | Units | Hours used | Contribution (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C | 3,000 | 6,000 | 1,80,000 |
| A | 2,000 | 8,000 | 1,60,000 |
| B | 500 | 4,000 | 60,000 |
| **Total** |  | 18,000 | 4,00,000 |
| Less fixed costs |  |  | (2,50,000) |
| **Profit** |  |  | 1,50,000 |

B has the highest contribution per unit (₹120) but the lowest per machine hour (₹15), so it gets only the hours left over: 4,000 hours = 500 units.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a fixed budget and a flexible budget. Why is a flexible budget better for control?
questions.answer:
- A **fixed budget** is prepared for one level of activity and is not changed when actual activity differs.
- A **flexible budget** is designed to change with activity; costs are classified as fixed, variable and semi-variable, and the budget is recast for the actual level.
- Fixed budgets suit stable conditions and fixed-cost areas; flexible budgets suit businesses with varying output.
- Comparing actual cost with a fixed budget at a different activity level mixes volume effects with efficiency effects, so variances are misleading.
- A flexible budget compares actual cost with what cost should have been at the actual output, so variances reflect spending and efficiency, and managers are held responsible fairly.
- Flexible budgets also help in pricing and in setting overhead rates at different levels.

questions.prompt: State the limitations of marginal costing.
questions.answer:
- Splitting costs into fixed and variable is difficult; many costs are semi-variable.
- Stock is valued at variable cost only, which understates it and is not accepted for financial statements, which require production overheads in inventory.
- Ignoring fixed costs in pricing can lead to prices that do not cover total cost in the long run.
- Contribution analysis assumes constant prices, variable cost per unit and sales mix, which rarely hold.
- It gives less attention to the time factor: two jobs with equal contribution may take different machine time.
- In capital-intensive industries, fixed costs are large and cannot be ignored in decisions.
